Q. For hundreds of years in the early history of America, pirates sailed through coastal waters, pillaging and plundering all in their path. They stole from other ships and stole from coastal towns; not content only to steal, they destroyed everything they could not carry away. Some of the pirate ships amassed large treasures, the fates of which are unknown, leaving people of today to wonder at their where about and to dream of one day coming across some lost treasure.

One notoriously large treasure was on the pirate ship Whidah, which sank in the waters off Cape Cod during a strong storm in 1717. A hundred of the crew members went down with the ship, along with its treasure of coins, gold, silver, and jewels. The treasure on board had an estimated value, on today's market, of more than 100 million dollars.

The remains of the Whidah were discovered in 1984 by Barry Clifford, who had spent years of painstaking research and tireless searching, only finally to locate the ship about 500 yards from shore. A considerable amount of treasure from the centuries-old ship has been recovered from its watery grave, but there is clearly still a lot more out there. Just as a reminder of what the waters off the coast have been protecting for hundreds of years, occasional pieces of gold or silver or jewels still wash up on the beaches and lucky beach-goers find pieces of the treasure.

Q. It is a characteristic of human nature that people like to get together and have fun, and people living during America's frontier days were no exception. However, because life was hard and the necessities of day-to-day living took up their time, it was common for recreation to be combined with activities necessary for survival.

One example of such a form of recreation was logrolling. Many frontier areas were heavily wooded, and in order to settle an area it was necessary to remove the trees. A settler could cut down the trees alone, but help was needed to move the cut tress. After a settler had cut a bunch of tress, he would then invite his neighbors over for a logrolling.

A logrolling was a community event where families got together for a combination of of work and fun. The women would bring food and have a much needed and infrequent opportunity to relax and chat with friends, the children would play together exuberantly, and the men would hold lively competition that involved rolling logs from place to place as quickly as possible. This was a day of fun for everyone involved, but at its foundation was the need to clear the land.

Q. Quite different from storm surges are the giant waves called Tsunamis, which derive their name from Japanese expression for "high water in a harbor". These waves are also referred to by the general public as tidal waves, although they have relatively little to do with tides. Scientist often refer to them as seismic sea waves, far more appropriate in that they do result from undersea seismic activity.

Tsunami are caused when the sea bottom suddenly moves, during an underwater earthquake or volcano, for example, and the water above the moving earth is suddenly displaced. This sudden shift of water sets off a series of waves. These waves can travel great distances at speed close to 700 Kilometers per hour. In the open ocean, tsunamis have little noticeable amplitude, often no more than one or two meters. it is when they hit the shallow waters near the coast that they increase in height, possibly up to 40 meters.

Tsunamis often occur in the Pacific because the Pacific is an area of heavy seismic activity. Two areas of the Pacific well accustomed to the threat of tsunamis are Japan and Hawaii. Because the seismic activity that causes tsunamis in Japan often occurs on the ocean bottom quite close to the islands, the tsunamis that hit Japan often come with little warning and can therefore prove disastrous. Most of the tsunamis that hit the Hawaiian islands, however, originate thousands of miles away near the coast of Alaska, so these tsunamis have much greater distance to travel and the inhabitants of Hawaii generally have time for warning of their imminent arrival.

Tsunamis are certainly not limited to Japan and Hawaii. 1755, Europe experienced a calamitous tsunami, when movement along the fault lines near the Azores caused massive tsunami to sweep onto Portuguese coast and flood the heavily populated area around Lisbon. The greatest tsunami on record occured on the other side of the world in 1883 when the Krakatoa volcano underwent a massive explosion, sending waves more than 30 meters high onto nearby Indonesian island; the tsunami from this volcano actually traveled around the world and was witnessed as far away as the English Channel.

Welcome to the American Literature Museum’s exhibit on Gone with the Wind, featuring Margaret Mitchell’s original manuscript for the book, several drafts of Sidney Howard’s script for the movie, and many costumes from the movie set. This flier is intended to give you a brief orientation of the exhibit.
Background
Mitchell’s only novel published in her lifetime is one of the best-selling books of all time in the United States. It portrays the life of a wealthy American family in the pre–Civil War South, as well as during and after the war. The movie, based on Mitchell’s novel, would also become as successful as the book.
Gallery A: The Life of Margaret Mitchell and the Writing of Gone with the Wind
This section features photographs, correspondence, and personal items from Mitchell’s life. Of particular interest is a manuscript for a novel she wrote before Gone with the Wind, called Lost Laysen, which was first published in 1996, long after the author’s death.
Gallery B: Gone with the Wind, the Movie
Three years after Mitchell’s novel was published in 1936, it was made into a movie that won 10 Academy Awards. Three of the awards are on display in this gallery. Many original costumes are featured, including the intricate dresses and hats that Vivien Leigh, the actress who portrayed Scarlett O’Hara, wore. Some of the drafts of Howard’s script are also on display. One interesting thing to note is that if his first draft had been used, the movie would have been five and a half hours long.
Gallery C: Life in the Old South
This gallery features photographs and drawings of life in the pre–Civil War South. In contrast to the mostly rosy picture that the novel and movie portray, this exhibit gives a more realistic picture of the time. Of special interest are old audio recordings of folk songs that first appeared during the era. These songs were not written down but were passed from generation to generation.

The term “neon light” was originally applied to a particular type of vapor lamp using the inert, colorless gas neon. A long tube was filled with neon, which then became luminous at low pressure when an electric current was passed through it. The lamp then emitted the characteristic reddish-orange light of neon. Today, the term “neon light” is given to lamps of this general type which may be filled with a variety of gases, depending on the color that is desired. Argon, for example, is used to produce blue light. Colors can also be altered by changing the color of the glass tube. The tubes must be quite long in all these lamps to produce light efficiently. As a result, high voltages are required. Neon tube lamps are not practical for indoor illumination, but they have found widespread outdoor use in glowing, colorful advertising signs.

Q. What is the function of this sentence " In John Naughton’s article “Working from home was the dream but is it turning into a nightmare?” published in The Guardian , the author discusse s the work from home issue (WFH) and its consequences."?

Q. What is the writer talking about here:
" The author starts with remind ing the reader that WFH was once an option tha t many people wished for , and with the COVID19 situation, it has become the new normal. While people thought that WFH would provide them with a better work-life balance, the author argues that it has actually caused less balance. The author , then, discusses the difficulties people faced working from home such as the lack of resour ces ( laptops, strong broadband networks, and workspaces ) and the inability to look after the kids when nurseries and schools were shut down. Naughton continues to say that even if some people managed to deal with such difficulties, WFH was not the best option for them. People had to work more hours, get into back-to-back meetings, and work seemed to invade people’ homes rather than save them the commute time as they thought before. The author adds that employers have even started to use surveillance tools to monitor employees at home and make sure they are on task throughout the day , ending with the old proverb “be careful what you wish for, you might just get it!”. Indeed, Naughton has managed to lay out his argument logically and provided good support for his viewpoint ; however, he may have had some logical fallacies and may have overlooked the opposing point of view , making his argument l ess convincing than intended."?

Q. Where is the thesis statement in this introductory paragraph?

" In John Naughton’s article “Working from home was the dream but is it turning into a nightmare?” published in The Guardian , the author discusse s the work from home issue (WFH) and its consequences. The author starts with remind ing the reader that WFH was once an option tha t many people wished for , and with the COVID19 situation, it has become the new normal. While people thought that WFH would provide them with a better work-life balance, the author argues that it has actually caused less balance. The author , then, discusses the difficulties people faced working from home such as the lack of resour ces ( laptops, strong broadband networks, and workspaces ) and the inability to look after the kids when nurseries and schools were shut down. Naughton continues to say that even if some people managed to deal with such difficulties, WFH was not the best option for them. People had to work more hours, get into back-to-back meetings, and work seemed to invade people’ homes rather than save them the commute time as they thought before. The author adds that employers have even started to use surveillance tools to monitor employees at home and make sure they are on task throughout the day , ending with the old proverb “be careful what you wish for, you might just get it!”. Indeed, Naughton has managed to lay out his argument logically and provided good support for his viewpoint ; however, he may have had some logical fallacies and may have overlooked the opposing point of view , making his argument l ess convincing than intended. "

Q. What is the writer talking about here? Where is the topic sentence in this paragraph? Why does the writer use quotes here?

"Naughton's argument is clear from the title: WFH is a dream that is turning into a nightmare. The author’s claim is stated explicitly in saying “ I’m picking up a distinct impression that the novelty of WFH has begun to wear thin . . . the more acute our perceptions of its implications and downsides are becoming”, where he asserts that people’s liking for the WFH option is fading away with time passing by and showing the downsides of WFH. Naughton provides several reasons for his claim. He starts with the normal “glitches” that faced some people at the beginning: “Childcare, for example, became a nightmare when schools and nurseries closed . . . And there were still large numbers of “critical” workers whose work couldn’t be done from home”. Then, he moves on to the two main reasons behind his belief that WFH has negatively affected people’s lives. The first reason for Naughton’s belief is the shift in the work-life balance in favour of the office as he asserts that people work harder while working from home. Naughton’s second reason behind thinking that WFH is turning into a nightmare is the invasion of people’s homes with the surveillance tools deployed by the employers to ensure productivity and efficiency while working from home."

Q. What is this paragraph about? Does the writer use quotes here?

In supporting his reasons, Naughton uses a variety of evidence. He starts with anecdotes “I’ve lost count of the number of colleagues and friends who confess to being “Zoomed out” at the end of a day” . He also uses logical reasoning in “it turns out that online meetings are more cognitively demanding because, in the absence of physical cues, one simply has to concentrate more … meetings can be scheduled back to back – and many are” . In addition, Naughton refers to an expert ’s opinion when he quotes MG Siegler , a venture capitalist in “ It’s about the world in which we currently live, which has made work from home a necessity . . . to make this world as efficient as possible”. He also cites a large-scale study with numbers and statistics on the effect of WFH on the number of work meetings and the duration of the work day during the pandemic. For the second reason, Naughton refers to a report by Wired to support his claim concerning the privacy issue “For example, last week Wired reported : “Programs such as Time Doctor, ActivTrak, . . . have all seen huge increases in demand ”. Moreover, h e cites an authority figure: “ According to the Information Commissioner’s Office, employers must tell employees . . . being informed about the extent of the snooping” to show that the issue is considered a serious intrusion of privacy.

Q. What is the writer talking about here?

In fact, throughout, Naughton provides sufficient and relevant evidence to support his claim ; however, the evidence ma y not be typical or accurate enough in some instances . He seems to depend on evidence from personal observations and anecdotes rather than on facts and statistics . H e refers to one study only from one countr y which may not be generalizable to the wider population in other countries around the world . He cites a report from Wired and a quote by a governmental authority while he could have cited testimonies of employees or other large-scale studies to further strengthen his claim. For the sources, Naughton seems to have cited reliable and relevant sources, and there is also a hyper link for each of the sources (MG Siegler , the large-scale study and Wired) that he uses in the article.

Q. What is this paragraph about?

The author’s use of appeals is quite clear in the article. He appeals to the reader’s emotions in most of the article. His choice of words makes the reader feel much resentment against WFH. This is evident in words and expressions such as: “ nightmare”, “invade”, “sinister”, “naive belief”, “stay chained to their laptops”, “snooping”, and “intruding” . N au ghton also appeals to reason when he cites evidence from studies, statistics, experts , and anecdotes as discussed above. He does not use ethos that much in the article, though. He does not refer to his expertise in the field, and only refer s to one reliable source of information which is the Information Commissioner’s Office . In addition, it seems that the author do es not consider the opposing point of view that WFH does have some economic and social merits and that it actually helps people avoid exposing themselves to the risk of contracting the virus in the physical work environment. Hence, the author is not balanced in his use of appeals.

Q. What is paragraph about?

While Naughton has managed to provide good support for his argument, he relies on hasty generalisations in saying “I’ve lost count of the number of colleagues . . . being “Zoomed out” at the end of a day”. If this is the case with the author’s friends and family, it does not necessarily apply to everyone else. In addition, the author cites evidence from a single person as an expert witness: “Morning meetings bleed into afternoon meetings . . . writes MG Siegler , a venture capitalist who currently works from home”. Siegler’s experience may not be true to everyone else even if this is true for him as an authority figure. In addition, this is considered an appeal to false authority as Naughton could have cited more relevant experts such as psychologists, sociologists or even the employees themselves.

Q. What is the function of this paragraph?

In conclusion, Naughton has succeed ed in presenting his argument and use d good evidence to support it, but he seems to have had some logical fallacies, and there seems to be some weaknesses in his use of appeals . He has provided tw o main reasons to support his argument against WFH: the lack of work-life balance and the intrusion of employees’ privacy at home through surveillance tools. Overall, the author has managed to tickle the reader’s emotions, and the article seems to be convincing, especially that it is a current topic that affects many people around the world.

Q. Alliteration draws attention to a string of words through the repetition of their initial sounds.

Q. Analogy is a comparison between items that share a similarity, but are actually quite different.
Ex: Seasons of life; life is a highway
Q. Exaggeration emphasizes a fact through hyperbole. Ex: The wait until Christmas seemed like an eternity.

Q. Imagery an appeal to one or more of the senses by creating a vivid impression through the use of details and figures of speech like metaphors, simile, personification.
Ex: Fingers of fear ran down his spine

Q. Parallelism repeats specific words, phrases or clauses in a series, giving key emphasis to key words, making them memorable. Ex: Abraham Lincoln said government was “of the people, by the people, for the people.”
Q. Repetition is used for emphasis and rhythm. Ex: It was a strange night, a hushed night, a moonless night.
Q. Rhetorical Question is one whose answer is already known or implied. Ex: You don’t expect me to do homework on the weekend, do you?
Q. Sentence Fragments place emphasis on key words to create an overall effect, such as humor or suspense. Ex: A dark day. A dreary day. Typical for gray and cold November.
Q. Understatement creates the reverse effect and adds a touch of irony, by making the fact seem less important. Ex: Bruce Willis’s onscreen characters frequently find themselves in a bit of a jam.

Q. Ad hominem –attacking the opponent, rather than his/her arguments. The idea is that if the opponent is discredited, the listener will dismiss his/her arguments too. For example: Anyone who agrees with capital punishment is a murderer at heart.
Q. Appeals to Emotion are often used to manipulate the listener without using sound reasoning, logic or evidence. Ex: Appeal to fear
Q. Bandwagon – suggesting that an idea has merit because many people believe in it. For example: Millions of people eat at McDonald’s so the food must be good.
Q. Hasty generalization –A generalized claim that may not be true for all. EX: All Canadians love snow.

Q. Insufficient Evidence (Hasty Generalizations– The speaker may make claims that are generalized and based on a small sample, and will suggest that the data has greater significance than it really does. For example: My grandfather smoked a pack a day and lived to be eighty-five; therefore smoking does not kill.

Q. Slippery Slope -- The speaker begins with a statement and builds his/her claim to an alarming proclamation. The intent is to arouse fear in the listener, so much so that they miss the leaps in logic.
